title: Grammar Flexibility for IELTS Speaking
grammar_goal: Boosts Speaking GRA to Band 7+ by demonstrating the ability to effortlessly switch between past, present, and future tenses, as well as use hypothetical structures naturally in spoken English.

core_rule.formula: Mix Tenses: Present Perfect (experience) -> Past Simple (detail) -> Future (prediction) -> Conditional (hypothetical)
core_rule.usage: In Speaking, particularly Parts 2 and 3, examiners listen for your ability to maneuver through different timeframes seamlessly. You must not get stuck using only the Present Simple.

when_to_use: Speaking Part 1: Contrasting the past with the present (e.g., 'I used to play tennis, but nowadays I prefer jogging.').
Speaking Part 2: Telling a story correctly using Narrative Tenses (Past Simple for main events, Past Continuous for background, Past Perfect for prior events).
Speaking Part 3: Speculating about the future (e.g., 'In 50 years, people will probably be living on Mars.').
when_not_to_use: Do not overcomplicate your grammar so much that you lose fluency. It is better to use Past Simple accurately than to stumble while trying to use Past Perfect Continuous.

ielts_examples.speaking: Well, I've been living in this city for five years now. Before that, I lived in a small village, and to be honest, if I have the chance, I would love to move back there someday.
ielts_examples.writing: (This lesson focuses specifically on spoken flexibility, but tense accuracy applies everywhere.)

repair_section.wrong: I live here since 2015. Before I live in Hanoi.
repair_section.correct: I have lived here since 2015. Before that, I lived in Hanoi.
repair_section.better_band_upgrade: I've been residing here since 2015; prior to that, I was based in Hanoi.

repair_section.wrong: When I was a child, I am playing outside every day.
repair_section.correct: When I was a child, I played outside every day.
repair_section.better_band_upgrade: Back in my childhood, I used to spend hours playing outdoors on a daily basis.

vietnamese_learner_mistakes: Tense rigidity: Sticking to Present Simple for an entire 2-minute Part 2 monologue that asks about a past event.
Dropping past tense endings: Pronouncing 'played' as 'play' or 'watched' as 'watch', causing the examiner to mark it as a grammar/pronunciation error.
Using 'will' for everything in the future, missing the chance to use 'might', 'could', or 'is going to'.

mini_sentence_repair_exercise.wrong_sentence: I have gone to Paris last year.
mini_sentence_repair_exercise.correct_sentence: I went to Paris last year.

mini_sentence_repair_exercise.wrong_sentence: If I am rich in the future, I travel the world.
mini_sentence_repair_exercise.correct_sentence: If I am rich in the future, I will travel the world.

image_prompt_fallback: A vibrant, abstract image of a clock face melting or shifting, representing the fluidity of time and the ability to move between past, present, and future tenses.

quiz.question: Which response to the Speaking Part 1 question 'Do you like reading?' demonstrates the best tense flexibility?

options.A: Yes, I like reading. I read every day. Reading is good.
options.B: Yes, I like reading. I read a book yesterday. I will read tomorrow.
options.C: Absolutely. I've always been an avid reader. I used to read mostly fiction when I was younger, but lately I've been focusing on biographies.
options.D: Yes, I am reading books. I was reading a book. I had read a book.

quiz.explanation: Option C flows naturally and demonstrates Present Perfect ('ve always been'), 'used to' for past habits, and Present Perfect Continuous ('ve been focusing') to describe a recent ongoing change.
